newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU says not trying to curb barley sales to Saudis.
newsitem.headline: EU says not trying to curb barley sales to Saudis.

text.p: The European Union is not trying to prevent exporters from finalising barley sales clinched with Saudi Arabia, but a weaker U.S. dollar limits its scope in granting export subsidies, a European Union grain official said.
Some traders, scrambling to deliver barley they have pledged to the Saudis on time, would like the European Union to award higher export subsidies for barley to make up for a fall in the U.S. dollar.
But the EU is torn between helping cover the sales and keeping its finances under control.
"We have no intention of restricting our barley exports to Saudi Arabia but we must respect certain criteria," the official said.
"The fall in the dollar is making the situation more difficult than it was three weeks to a month ago...Raising the (refund) threshold is costly, so we are being more careful," he added.
Traders estimate that after the dollar's fall, last week's EU refund of 31 Ecus per tonne was insufficient to help cover the Saudi sale. They are seeking a refund of at least 35 Ecus.
But the official said the 31 Ecu refund, which valued UK barley at $130 per tonne, FOB, was sufficient to help cover exports to Saudi Arabia.
Exporters sold 1.4 million tonnes of October-December barley to Saudi Arabia in late September for $146-$158 a tonne, including freight.
The EU, which enjoys a freight and supply advantage over other world suppliers, was initially expected to supply 700,000 tonnes of barley, including 500,000 tonnes from the free market.
Canada, the U.S. and Turkey were also expected to help cover the sale.
But exporters now put the EU share of the Saudi contract at 800,000 to 900,000 tonnes, citing logistical and weather problems experienced by some of the other potential suppliers.

The Commission has already helped cover a large part of the Saudi sale. But it cannot be held responsible if exporters who initially bet on cheaper origins are now turning to the EU for export licences at a time when the dollar is weak, the official said.
Since July 1, EU barley export commitments have reached two million tonnes, with a large part earmarked for the Saudis, he said.
Last week traders bid through France to export some 636,000 tonnes of free market barley at subsidies ranging from 31.00 to 39.97 Ecus per tonne.
But the EU only awarded 30,000 tonnes at a refund of 31 Ecus.
Traders, whose bids were rejected last week, are widely expected to apply again for licences at this week's EU grain tenders.
